Declared cross-file leakage, recorded at the HIGHEST value seen across environments. The ratchet forbids only growth, so a machine that leaks less still passes — and CI, lacking some packages this container has, stubs more of them and leaks more. 2026-08-05: rose from 7 files / 11 env / 26 added to 19 / 36 / 35. Leakage did not grow — the detector's scope did. It hooked only pytest_runtest_protocol, which fires after collection has already imported every test module, so every module-scope os.environ[...] and sys.modules[...] write in the repository sat inside the plugin's own baseline and was structurally invisible. It now brackets each module's import as well. The gap cost a full-suite collection abort (test_checkpoint.py set REDIS_URL to the empty string; dashboard/app.py rightly refuses to import on that) which this plugin watched happen and could not see. The same widening also surfaced two real module-identity collisions on the generic names `app` and `introspect_app`, both now scoped.

2026-08-05 (2): merged GitHub-runner observations from run 30978117360. Six files stub more there than here — CI lacks packages this container has installed, so their absent-dependency stubs actually fire. Two (test_audio_service, test_tts_service) leak in CI and not at all locally. Recorded at the per-file MAXIMUM, which is what this baseline has always meant: a machine that leaks less still passes, and a baseline recorded on one machine alone fails the other forever on a difference that is not a defect. `replaced` is 0 in both environments, which is the count that is actually enforced.
known_limitation: The `added` and `env_set` ratchets are only as tight as the LOOSEST environment. A file that leaks 0 here and 5 in CI is baselined at 5, so a genuine new local leak of 1..5 in that file passes unnoticed. This is accepted, not overlooked. `replaced` is the load-bearing invariant — it is 0 and enforced everywhere, and it is the class that took the whole suite down. `added` is declared debt, and the marginal value of tightening it does not justify per-environment baselines keyed on a package fingerprint: a new fingerprint would silently create a new un-ratcheted environment, which is the same hole wearing a hat. The right way to close it is to make the environments match so the baselines converge, not to add machinery here. Revisit if a local-only leak is ever observed causing a problem.
